::: {.why}
Two autocorrelation functions from the same series, one flat and one decaying slowly, and every volatility model in this course exists because of that pair of facts.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State what near-zero return autocorrelation rules out, and what strongly positive absolute-return autocorrelation rules out, and say what the two jointly imply about any model of returns.
- Give the approximate decay behaviour of the absolute-return autocorrelation and say what it rules out about the memory of the process.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>55 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Quantify what you plotted last night: report the lag-1 through lag-5 autocorrelation of returns with confidence bands, then the same for absolute returns and for squared returns, out to lag 100. Fit the decay of the absolute-return ACF and say whether it looks geometric or slower.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Show that the two facts are compatible: simulate a series with independent signs and a slowly varying volatility level, and reproduce both autocorrelation functions. Getting this simulation right is the mental model you will use for GARCH in week 13, four weeks before you meet it.
:::
:::
